4                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                       
5                     NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                     
6                            SAN JOSE DIVISION                            
7                                                                         
8    MAXIMILIAN KLEIN, et al.,        Case No.  20-cv-08570-LHK (VKD)     

9              Plaintiffs,                                                
                                      ORDER RE SEPTEMBER 28, 2021         
10          v.                         DISPUTE RE PLAINTIFFS' INITIAL      
                                      DISCLOSURES                         
11    FACEBOOK, INC.,                                                      
                                      Re: Dkt. No. 156                    
               Defendant.                                                 
12                                                                         

13                                                                         
14        The Advertiser Plaintiffs1 and the Consumer Plaintiffs2 (collectively, “Plaintiffs”) and 
15   defendant Facebook, Inc. (“Facebook”) ask the Court to resolve their dispute regarding the 
16   sufficiency of Plaintiffs’ Rule 26(a) initial disclosures regarding computation of damages.  Dkt. 
17   No. 156.  The Court finds this matter suitable for resolution without a hearing.  See Civil L.R. 7-
18   1(b).                                                                 
19        For the reasons explained below, the Court concludes that the Consumer Plaintiffs must 
20   supplement their initial disclosures, but the Advertiser Plaintiffs need not. 
21   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
22        Facebook contends that Plaintiffs have not disclosed the amount or method for computing 
23   damages or the documents or evidence on which they intend to rely, as required by Rule 26(a).  
24   Facebook points to Plaintiffs’ representations that they have already extensively investigated their 
25   respective claims and developed their theories of liability.  In addition, Facebook observes that 
26   Plaintiffs have had access to more than 12 million documents relating to their claims for five 
27                                                                         
1   months.  Plaintiffs respond that they have made the required disclosures, and that Facebook’s 
2   demands exceed what Rule 26(a) requires.  In particular, Plaintiffs argue that their damages 
3   disclosures are commensurate with the information reasonably available to them at this stage of 
4   the case.  They point out that a more precise computation of damages will likely require expert 
5   testimony, and they note that Facebook’s document production to date does not include all of the 
6   records necessary for a more complete damages analysis.               
7   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
8        Rule 26(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure requires that each party “provide . . . a 
9   computation of each category of damages claimed by the . . . party—who must also make 
10   available for inspection and copying as under Rule 34 the documents or other evidentiary material, 
11   unless privileged or protected from disclosure, on which each computation is based, including 
12   materials bearing on the nature and extent of injuries suffered[.]”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)(iii).  
13   Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(iii) does not require damages to be calculated with precision.  However, it does 
14   require a plaintiff to disclose its computation of damages, in light of the information currently 
15   available to it, in sufficient detail so as to enable the defendant to understand its potential exposure 
16   and to make informed decisions about discovery and other matters.  E.g., City & County of San 
17   Francisco v. Tutor-Saliba Corp., 218 F.R.D. 219, 221 (N.D. Cal. 2003); see also Song v. 
18   Drenberg, No. 18-cv-06283-LHK (VKD), 2019 WL 1949785, at *1 (N.D. Cal. May 2, 2019) 
19   (discussing initial disclosures generally).  A party is not excused from making these disclosures 
20   because it has not fully investigated the case.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(E). 
21        Because their respective disclosures differ, the Court separately considers whether the 
22   Advertiser Plaintiffs and the Consumer Plaintiffs have complied with the requirements of Rule 
23   26(a)(1)(A)(iii).                                                     
24        A.   Advertiser Plaintiffs                                       
25        The Advertiser Plaintiffs’ initial damages disclosure states that they seek compensatory 
26   damages arising from overcharges for advertising.  The disclosure describes the methodology used 
27   to compute damages and gives an estimate of the amount of damages on behalf of the plaintiff 
1   damages.  The disclosure specifically identifies some documents used to compute damages and 
2   states that others will be produced before September 10, 2021.  Dkt. No. 156-2 at 26-28. 
3        Facebook objects that this disclosure is based on an improper or inapplicable methodology 
4   for computing damages, and that the Advertiser Plaintiffs fail to adequately support their claim 
5   that they were overcharged.  To the extent Facebook challenges the merits of the Advertiser 
6   Plaintiffs’ methodology, its objection is not well-taken; the Advertiser Plaintiffs have disclosed 
7   their methodology, which is all that Rule 26(a) requires.  To the extent Facebook challenges the 
8   disclosure as lacking support, if the Advertiser Plaintiffs have disclosed the remaining documents 
9   on which they rely, as they stated they would before September 10, 2021, then the Court is not 
10   persuaded that they have failed to identify the supporting evidentiary material as the Rule requires. 
11        Both parties acknowledge that expert testimony may be necessary for a full disclosure of 
12   the Advertiser Plaintiffs’ damages computation.  However, the fact that such testimony may be 
13   necessary, or that the Court has set a separate deadline for the disclosure of expert testimony under 
14   Rule 26(a)(2), does not relieve the Advertiser Plaintiffs of their obligation to timely supplement 
15   their initial disclosures as their damages theories develop.   See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e)(1)(A); Tutor-
16   Saliba, 218 F.R.D. at 221, 222 (further specification of damages computation may require expert 
17   analysis or testimony).  On the record presented, the Court is unable to conclude that the 
18   Advertiser Plaintiffs have failed to disclose expert analysis supporting their damages computation 
19   that is reasonably available to them at this time.                    
20        B.   Consumer Plaintiffs                                         
21        The Consumer Plaintiffs’ initial damages disclosure states that they seek compensatory 
22   damages reflecting “the difference between the reduced value that Facebook provided Consumer 
23   Plaintiffs as a result of Facebook’s alleged competition-reducing conduct and the value that 
24   competition free of Facebook’s anticompetitive restraints would have required Facebook to 
25   provide Consumer Plaintiffs (including adequate compensation for the data that Consumer 
26   Plaintiffs provided to Facebook but which Facebook did not provide adequate consideration for in 
27   return).”  Dkt. No. 156-1 at 13.  However, apart from a reference to Facebook’s purported “market 
    1    Plaintiffs compute damages.  /d. at 13-14.  Instead, the disclosure refers in a superficial manner to 
    2  ||  “publicly-available documents” that the Consumer Plaintiffs say support a damages estimate of at 
    3    least “tens of billions of dollars.”  The Consumer Plaintiffs do not identity the documents or other 
    4  || evidentiary material on which they rely, and they make no representations about making 
    5  || producing these documents to Facebook.  See id. 
    6          The Court agrees with Facebook that this disclosure does not meet the requirements of 
    7    Rule 26(a)(1)(A)Gii).  If the Consumer Plaintiffs seek damages based on provision of user data 
    8    without adequate compensation, they must identify the data for which insufficient compensation 
    9    was provided and an estimate of its value, as well as the methodology used to compute the 
   10  ||  estimate and the evidentiary material on which they rely.  If the Consumer Plaintiffs seek damages 
   11    based on something other than the uncompensated value of their data, they must describe with 
    12  ||  greater specificity the nature of the harm for which they claim damages, the methodology on 
5    13    which they rely to compute damages, and an estimate of the amount of damages claimed.  In 
    14  ||  addition, the Consumer Plaintiffs must identify the documents or other evidentiary material on 
 3    15    which they base their damages computation or produce the materials to Facebook. 
     16          As noted above, the fact that expert testimony may be necessary for a full disclosure of the 
 3    17    Consumer Plaintiffs’ damages computation, does not relieve the Consumer Plaintiffs of their 
    18  || obligation to timely supplement their initial disclosures as their damages theories develop. 
   19  || 11.    CONCLUSION 
   20          The Consumer Plaintiffs must supplement their initial disclosures regarding damages by 
   21    November 3, 2021.  The Advertiser Plaintiffs need not supplement their disclosures at this time. 
   22          IT IS SO ORDERED. 
   23    Dated: October 13, 2021 
   24 

   6                                                    VIRGINIA K. DEMARCH 
                                                        United States Magistrate Judge
